stories.headline: STOCKS SHAKE OFF FRESH IRAN STRIKES TO CLOSE AT SESSION HIGHS
stories.body: The Dow fell more than 400 points intraday after Trump ordered new strikes on Iran, but all three major indexes reversed to close higher as Treasury yields eased — the S&P 500 gained 1.06% to 7,747.71, the Dow rose 1.18% to 53,686.11, and the Nasdaq 100 added 1.05% to 29,448. Oil and gold both stayed bid on safe-haven demand even as equities recovered.
stories.explain: Equities sold off on the initial headline because a wider Iran conflict raises the odds of a Strait of Hormuz disruption, which would spike energy costs and act like a tax on growth. The reversal came once traders judged Trump's comment that strikes would be 'short-lived' as capping tail risk, and falling yields lowered the discount rate used to value future earnings — a double tailwind for risk assets even with oil and gold still elevated.

stories.headline: FED CHAIR WARSH SIGNALS NO 2026 RATE CUTS AS SEPTEMBER ODDS FALL TO ZERO
stories.body: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated a data-dependent, no-cuts-in-2026 stance, and Fed funds futures now price essentially zero probability of a September cut from the current 3.50%-3.75% target range. Governor Waller said he'd lean toward holding unless inflation surprises to the upside.
stories.explain: Fed funds futures translate CME-traded contract prices into implied probabilities for each FOMC meeting, so a move to near-zero odds means the market has fully repriced away easing expectations that existed earlier this year. That repricing matters because it removes a tailwind that had been supporting duration-sensitive assets like growth stocks and long bonds — the 10-year's dip to 4.76% today came despite the hawkish Fed talk, driven instead by the Iran-related flight to safety.

stories.headline: ADP SHOWS PRIVATE PAYROLLS SLOWING TO 38K, MISSING ESTIMATES AHEAD OF FRIDAY'S JOBS REPORT
stories.body: ADP reported U.S. private employers added just 38,000 jobs in August, below the 47,000 consensus and down from an upwardly revised 46,000 in July. Factory orders were a bright spot, up 0.9% versus a 0.7% estimate.
stories.explain: ADP is a leading, imperfect proxy for Friday's official nonfarm payrolls report, so a miss here shifts market expectations toward a softer NFP print and reinforces the labor-market-cooling narrative the Fed is watching under its dual mandate. A weak jobs number would normally build the case for rate cuts, but with Warsh signaling no cuts regardless, the more likely market reaction is concern about growth rather than relief on policy.

stories.headline: GOLD SURGES PAST $4,490 AS OIL HOLDS NEAR $91 ON STRAIT OF HORMUZ RISK
stories.body: Gold jumped over 2% on safe-haven buying as the Iran conflict escalated, while WTI held near $91 and Brent near $95 after cooling from a three-day, 9% rally. Kuwait reported it was fending off Iranian missile and drone attacks, keeping traders focused on shipping risk through the Strait of Hormuz.
stories.explain: About one-fifth of global oil supply transits the Strait of Hormuz, so any credible threat to that chokepoint gets priced immediately into the crude forward curve as a geopolitical risk premium, distinct from actual supply loss. Gold's rally reflects the same dynamic in reverse — it carries no counterparty risk and tends to draw capital whenever investors fear an escalation that could disrupt normal markets, which is why it moved in lockstep with oil today rather than with the dollar, which slipped slightly to 99.51 on the DXY.

stories.headline: AI NAMES POWER NASDAQ RALLY AS SNOWFLAKE JUMPS 20%, NVIDIA MOVES TO BUY HUGGING FACE
stories.body: Snowflake soared more than 20% on a blowout quarter, Dell rose 15.8% and GitLab gained 10%, while Nvidia agreed to acquire AI platform Hugging Face. Broadcom fell despite beating analyst estimates, a reminder that guidance can matter more than the headline beat.
stories.explain: Broadcom's drop on an earnings beat is a classic 'sell the news' pattern: when a stock has already run up into a print on high expectations, the market is really trading forward guidance and margin trajectory, not the trailing quarter's numbers. Snowflake and Dell's gains show the opposite case — results that beat a more conservative bar left room for the stock to re-rate higher, which is why identical-looking 'beats' can produce opposite price reactions.

stories.headline: NBA CHAMPION MICHAEL MALONE TAKES OVER AT NORTH CAROLINA AS ELIGIBILITY CHAOS CONTINUES
stories.body: Michael Malone, who won an NBA title as Denver's head coach, held his first preseason press conference leading North Carolina's program, saying 'the rules change every day' in college athletics. A wave of court injunctions has granted several players a fifth year of eligibility, adding roster uncertainty across the sport 101 days before tip-off.

stories.headline: CLIPPERS STRIPPED OF FIVE FIRST-ROUND PICKS, BALLMER FINED $30 MILLION IN KAWHI LEONARD CAP PROBE
stories.body: The NBA concluded its salary-cap circumvention investigation by stripping the Clippers of five first-round draft picks and fining owner Steve Ballmer $30 million over an alleged no-show sponsorship deal that funneled money to Kawhi Leonard. The SEC is separately reviewing sponsor Aspiration's former dealings with the team.

stories.headline: ALL 32 TEAMS SET 53-MAN ROSTERS AS LEAGUE HEADS INTO WEEK 1
stories.body: Cutdown day wrapped across the league with the regular season opening September 9. Kirk Cousins was named the Raiders' Week 1 starter, and the Rams and 49ers will play next week's game at Melbourne Cricket Ground as the NFL expands its international slate.

stories.headline: COLLEGE FOOTBALL KICKS OFF: COACH PRIME'S COLORADO VISITS GEORGIA TECH IN WEEK 1 OPENER
stories.body: Deion Sanders leads Colorado into Atlanta to face Georgia Tech for the second straight season in tonight's headline Week 1 matchup. Also playing: No. 7 Miami at Stanford and Fresno State at No. 14 USC, with No. 25 Missouri and No. 21 Utah opening at home.

deepDive.title: How a Geopolitical Risk Premium Gets Priced Into Oil and Gold
content: Today's session was a live case study in risk pricing: the Dow dropped over 400 points on news of fresh U.S. strikes on Iran, then clawed all the way back to close up 1.18% once yields eased and Trump signaled the escalation would be brief. Meanwhile oil held near $91 and gold jumped past $4,490, both refusing to give back their gains even as stocks recovered. That divergence — equities shrugging off the headline while commodities stayed bid — is exactly what you'd expect if markets are pricing a persistent risk premium rather than reacting to a one-day scare.

The mechanism runs through the futures curve. Oil traders don't just ask 'how much crude is being produced today' — they price the probability-weighted cost of disruption to the roughly one-fifth of global supply that transits the Strait of Hormuz. Even a modest chance of a shipping interruption gets baked into near-dated contracts as a premium over the 'fundamental' price implied by supply and demand alone, which is why WTI can hold near $91 even without a single barrel actually being lost. Gold works through a parallel but opposite channel: it has no yield and no industrial disruption risk, so it becomes the default parking spot for capital fleeing uncertainty, moving in the same direction as oil's risk premium rather than against it.

History shows this premium can be large and can also evaporate fast. After the September 2019 drone and missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's Abqaiq facility knocked out roughly 5% of global oil supply overnight, Brent spiked nearly 15% in a single session — the largest one-day jump since the 1991 Gulf War — before retracing most of the move within three weeks once markets confirmed output was restored faster than feared. The lesson most investors miss is that the premium is about the tail risk being removed, not the base case being realized; prices can stay elevated for weeks even if the feared disruption never actually happens, simply because the option value of insurance against it doesn't disappear until the underlying threat clearly does.

For Chris's kind of question — what does this mean for portfolio construction and the next data points — the immediate read-through is Friday's jobs report and the Fed. A weak NFP print combined with sustained elevated oil prices creates a stagflationary-flavored setup that complicates Warsh's already-hawkish no-cuts stance, since energy costs feed directly into headline CPI even if core inflation stays contained. It's also the textbook case for why professional portfolios hold some allocation to gold or commodities: not because they reliably outperform in normal markets, but because they are among the few assets that tend to move independently of, or even against, equities exactly when a geopolitical shock hits.
